newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco plans gradually to liberalise power output.
newsitem.headline: Morocco plans gradually to liberalise power output.

text.p: Morocco's state-run electricity utility, to attract foreign private investors, said on Friday it plans gradually to liberalise the power generating sector by partly financing new projects.
Driss Benhima, chairman of the Office National d'Electricite (ONE), told delegates at a Euromoney capital markets and investment forum:
"To optimise the openness of the power production process to the private sector, the ONE is examining a new formula of financing future power projects."
The two-day forum, attended by nearly 400 delegates representing 18 countries and international organisations, discussed ways to upgrade and diversify Morocco's economy to attract foreign capital.
"In order to minimise the costs, the office would participate to the new firms' capital by ceding stakes in ONE's subsidiaries," Benhima said.
Design, construction and exploitation of future power plants will be placed in the hands of private operators, he said.

"For the existing steam power stations, the ONE plans to transform them into subsidiary companies (societe anonyme) before going public through floatation on the bourse, and transfer their management to private sector," he said.
He said the presence of private power producers on the market "will improve the efficiency of the sector, permit technology transfer and create a synergy inside other units under ONE's management."
Morocco's demand for electricity rose annually at an average 6.0 percent since 1985 to around 11 billion KW/H in 1996.

"To meet this increasing demand, the ONE plans to set up new production units to reinforce and extend its interconnected network to provide Morocco's 27 million inhabitants with sufficient electricity," Benhima said.

Last year, Morocco initiated a $1.5 billion concession accord with Asea Brown Boveri Energy Ventures CMS Generation aimed at doubling capacity of two units power plants in Jorf Lasfar on the Atlantic coast, to 1,320 megawatts by the year 2000.
The two companies will manage the power plants during 30 years during which they will sell electricity production to ONE and will pay the $1.5 billion over a 20-year period.
The industrial Casablanca centre, near Jorf Lasfar, consumes annually 25 percent of Morocco's total power output, Benhima told the meeting.
Established in Casablanca in 1963, the ONE has the monopoly of power generating, its transportation and distribution through a network of local agencies.
